title: Sahih Muslim
hook: Muslim's Sahih, known for its careful arrangement

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sahih al-Bukhari, and your line: the sound collection. Did you say something good, or keep quiet? Day one thousand one hundred fifty-three.

A desk, a lamp, and a stack of notes. One saying of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ has reached you along several different chains of narrators, and each one words it a little differently. One adds a detail. One gives the whole scene; another, only the saying. So where do they go in your book? Scattered, a piece here and a piece there, wherever each fits a topic? Or all together, side by side, so a reader can see every version at once and spot exactly where they differ? One scholar chose the second way, and it's what his book is known for. Today, Sahih Muslim.
screen: `ONE SAYING, SEVERAL CHAINS.` → `SCATTER THEM, OR GATHER THEM?` → `SAHIH MUSLIM.`

segments.voice: First, the man. Muslim ibn al-Hajjaj, from the city of Nishapur. Muslim here is his name, not only his faith. Tradition says he studied with al-Bukhari and held him in deep respect. Two students of the same science, two books with the same name, sahih, sound. Together they're called the two Sahihs. Second, the arrangement. Al-Bukhari sometimes divided a hadith across his book, a piece under each heading where it proved a point. Muslim, for the most part, kept a hadith in one place and then laid its chains and wordings next to each other. For a student, that's a gift. You can watch one saying travel down several roads and see the exact place where a word changes. That's the careful arrangement his book is known for. Third, the doorway. Before the hadith begin, Muslim wrote an introduction. In it he explains why he takes reports only from people known to be reliable, and he warns against passing things on carelessly. He records a saying of the scholar Abdullah ibn al-Mubarak: the chain of narrators is part of the religion, and without it, anyone could say whatever they liked. Everything this path covered last week, in one line. Fourth, one hadith from inside. In Muslim's book, the Prophet says that Allah does not look at your bodies or your faces, but looks at your hearts and your deeds. Hearts and deeds, together. Scholars have weighed the two Sahihs against each other, and not all of them came down on the same side. This path takes them as a pair.
screen: `MUSLIM IBN AL-HAJJAJ, OF NISHAPUR.` · `EVERY CHAIN, SIDE BY SIDE.` · `THE CHAIN IS PART OF THE RELIGION.` · `HEARTS AND DEEDS.`

segments.voice: The practice: read one from Muslim. Today's is the one you just heard. Allah does not look at your bodies or your faces, but at your hearts and your deeds. Settle, and breathe. Let the first half land. Recall the last time you sized someone up by how they looked: the clothes, the face, the car. Then turn it around. What did you spend on your appearance this week, and what did you spend on your heart? No verdict. Just look, the way you'd look at a receipt. If you pray, you can carry that hadith into your next prayer. The bell holds the time.
Sahih Muslim. The second of the two Sahihs, where each hadith's chains and wordings are gathered in one place, side by side. Today's word.
Your line: the second sahih. Today, do one good thing nobody will see, something for the heart and not the mirror. Tomorrow: the four Sunan. Day one thousand one hundred fifty-three.

howItsDone: Sunni Muslims study Sahih Muslim alongside Sahih al-Bukhari, and teachers often use its gathered chains to show students how one hadith came down in several wordings.

myth: Sahih Muslim is a summary of al-Bukhari's book
it's a separate collection, arranged his own way, with each hadith's chains gathered together.
Muslim wrote an introduction about taking reports only from the reliable
and it records the saying that the chain of narrators is part of the religion.
in this book, Allah looks at faces and bodies
the hadith says the opposite: not bodies or faces, but hearts and deeds.

fork.setup: you've collected one saying through several chains, each worded a little differently. how do you set them in your book?
options: keep one and throw out the rest.
set them all together, side by side.
fork.reveal: that's Muslim's way. a reader can watch one saying travel down several roads and see where the wording shifts.

original.note: here Muslim is a man's name: Muslim ibn al-Hajjaj.

trapdoor: what you thought: the second sahih means the second-best one.
what it means: the second of the two Sahihs, studied as a pair with al-Bukhari's.
what a scholar hears: a book prized for its order, each hadith's chains and wordings gathered in one place, opened by an introduction on why the chain matters.

notes: Ibn al-Mubarak's saying ('the isnad is part of the religion; were it not for the isnad, whoever wished would say whatever he wished') as recorded in the Muqaddimah of Sahih Muslim: confirm placement.
Muslim 2564 (Allah does not look at your bodies/forms but at your hearts and deeds): confirm number; some versions read 'bodies and forms', paraphrased here as 'bodies or faces'.
Tradition that Muslim studied with al-Bukhari: framed as tradition; confirm.
Description of Bukhari dividing hadith across chapters and Muslim gathering chains in one place: a general characterization; confirm it is fair.

'Scholars have weighed the two Sahihs against each other ... not all came down on the same side': refers to the classical debate (some Maghribi scholars preferring Muslim); kept vague under the claims rule. Confirm.
Ibn al-Mubarak's saying was also used on day 1060 (year 3); here it is tied to Muslim's introduction specifically. Cut if too close.
Trapdoor floor one names a misreading ('second-best'); the lesson does not rank the two books.
